## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1:** Guzik says Jacob had not actually taken anything from Laban. His wealth was simply growing faster than Laban's, and the sons' claim came from envy, which twists the truth. [EW] Matthew Henry (short commentary) says selfish people feel robbed by anything that goes to someone else, and greed can override family affection. [BH7] Barnes says Jacob's success stirred up envy and slander in Laban's sons. [BH7]

**v. 2:** Guzik says the sons' envy turned Laban against Jacob, though Laban had been pleased with the wage deal in Genesis 30:34. Envy brings strife and division with it (1 Cor 3:3; James 3:16). [EW] Barnes says Laban himself had grown cold toward Jacob. [BH7]

**v. 3:** Guzik sees three steps in God's leading: first a desire to go home (30:25), then a situation that became unbearable, then a direct word from God. God may lead people the same way today. The promise "I will be with you" was the key, because it let Jacob face Esau, who had sworn to kill him. [EW] Barnes says God now orders Jacob home and promises to protect him. [BH7] Henry says that when we move, we should look to God's command and promise, and if he is with us we need not fear. [BH15], [BH20]

**v. 4:** Barnes notes that Rachel is named first. [BH7]

**v. 5:** Guzik says God showed he was stronger than anything Laban could do, keeping his promise of Genesis 28:15. He compares Psalm 118:6. [EW]

**v. 6:** Guzik says Jacob believed he had treated Laban fairly and that his wives knew it. [EW]

**v. 7:** On "ten times":
- Ellicott: it simply means "a good many times." [BH7]
- Benson: it means "often." Laban, from envy and greed, kept breaking the agreement, and Jacob put up with each change. [BH7]
- Clarke: the old translations disagree. The Greek Septuagint reads "ten lambs." Augustine took it to mean five years' wages, at two lambings a year. Clarke's own view is that it is an open-ended number meaning "frequently," as in Leviticus 26:26. [SL7]

**v. 8:** Benson argues that no natural cause could have matched every change of terms without once failing, so God must have arranged it. [BH7]

**v. 9:** Guzik says God protected Jacob from Laban's cheating. [EW]

**v. 10:** Guzik says the breeding success of Genesis 30:37–43 was shown to Jacob in a dream. Jacob used clever farming methods, but God's blessing mattered more. [EW] Barnes says the dream credits the result to "the God of nature" rather than to Jacob's skill. [SL13]

**v. 11:** Constable says it is unclear when this dream happened. It probably came before, or was the same as, the message in v. 3. [SL13] Gill thinks the rams dream came at the start of Jacob's six years of service, and the "God of Bethel" message is a separate, later vision. The two are told together because they deal with the same matter. [BH13]

**v. 12:** Barnes says the second dream refers back to the first as something still going on, which encouraged Jacob to trust God for the journey home. [SL13]

**v. 13:** On who the "angel" is:
- Calvin: the angel can speak as God either because the Father showed himself through his Word in angel form, or because angels sent by God rightly speak his words. God names himself "of Bethel" to remind Jacob of his promise, not because he is limited to one place. [SL13]
- A note on the biblehub page: the words show the angel is "Jehovah Himself in a manifested form," not a created angel (compare Exodus 23:20–21). [BH13]
- Geneva Study Bible: "This angel was Christ." Jacob speaks as though his wives already knew this, which suggests he had taught them to fear God. [BH13]
- Poole: God mentions the vow to show he accepted it, remembers his people's service, and means to keep his promise. [BH13]
- Guzik: this is a call back to Bethel, like returning to "first love" in Revelation 2:4–5. It is good to remember where God met us, and he quotes Spurgeon that God "change[s] not." [EW]

**v. 14:** Guzik says Laban had already used up whatever his daughters might have inherited, so they were glad to leave. He adds that this may be the first time in a long while the sisters agreed, united against their father. [EW]

**v. 15:** Ellicott sees "a marked asperity" (real sharpness) in the sisters' words, and concludes that Laban had recently been stingy and grasping. [BH15] Poole reads it as "he treats us as if we had no more right to his estate than strangers." [BH15]

**v. 16:** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB) says the wives fully agree and show both love for their husband and godliness. It quotes Henry: real helpers will never hold their husbands back from what God calls them to do. [BH15] Guzik says Jacob might not have obeyed without their support. [EW]

**v. 17:** Guzik says the camels show both a quick departure and Jacob's wealth. [EW]

**v. 18:** Henry says Jacob acted honestly. He took only "the cattle of his getting" and did not try to make up his losses himself. [SL19]

**v. 19:**
- Benson: Laban was shearing the part of his flock kept by his sons, three days away. [BH19]
- One note on the page: the teraphim were small household gods shaped like people, worshipped as bringers of prosperity and consulted as oracles. [BH19]
- Another note: they were small, since Rachel could hide them in a camel saddle. Women may have used them as charms, and Rachel took them hoping they would bring prosperity. [BH19]
- Henry: Rachel "was not so honest as her husband." The idols were probably for worship, and he hopes she took them to show her father how foolish it was to trust gods that could not protect themselves. [BH19], [SL19]
- Another note: she had "a lingering attachment" to them, as keepsakes and as protection on the journey. [BH19]
- The Biblical Illustrator: she may have wanted to stop Laban using them to find out which way they had gone, or wanted their protection. [SL19]
- Barnes: Scripture is not interested in describing false worship in detail. [SL19]
- Guzik lists the possible motives: she worshipped them; she wanted to stop Laban using them for divination; they worked as title deeds; revenge; or a Jewish tradition that she wanted to keep her father from idolatry. [EW]

**v. 20:** "Deceived" is literally "stole the heart."
- Ellicott and Barnes: the heart was the seat of understanding, so the phrase means acting without Laban knowing. [BH20]
- Coffman: it means he deceived Laban's mind, like the American saying "stole him blind." [SL20]
- Poole: Jacob took away what Laban's heart was set on, namely his daughters, cattle and gods. [BH20]

**v. 21:** Barnes says "the river" is the Euphrates, about 70 miles from Haran, with Gilead about 300 miles beyond it. [BH20] Guzik gives nearly 300 miles from Haran to Gilead. He says the journey was harder emotionally than physically, since Jacob was leaving a "comfortable servitude." [EW]

**v. 22:** Barnes says the three days show that Laban's flocks were three days' journey from Jacob's. [BH20] Guzik ties the delay to the shearing in v. 19. [EW]

**v. 23:** Barnes says "brethren" means Laban's relatives and dependents. [BH20] Guzik says catching Jacob in Gilead shows how fast Jacob travelled and how determined Laban was. [EW]

**v. 24:** Guzik says the warning shows Laban really did mean to harm Jacob, and God protected Jacob through the dream. [EW]

**v. 25:** Guzik says Gilead was close to the Jordan and the promised land. [EW]

**vv. 26–28:** Guzik says Laban first tried to shame Jacob with a show of kindness (the farewell party he says he would have thrown), and turned to threats when that failed. "My sons and my daughters" means his grandchildren. [EW]

## 2. Where interpreters differ

I couldn't open any Lutheran, Wesleyan, Pentecostal or Baptist denominational sources. The differences below are between individual commentators, not proven denominational splits.

**v. 20 (was the secret escape wrong?):**
- Faulted: Guzik says the sneaking away showed Jacob did not trust God's promise and leaned on his own cleverness. He quotes Barnhouse that Jacob "sneaked away into the will of God instead of departing in triumph." [EW]
- Defended: JFB (labelled "Calvinist" by StudyLight) says events proved it was wise and necessary, since Laban might have held Jacob back by force or trickery. [BH20], [SL20] Henry says it was "honestly done" and that Jacob kept it secret so Laban couldn't stop or rob him. [SL19]
- StudyLight says 45 commentators split six ways on this verse. Its tradition counts are Calvinist 5, Arminian 2, Dispensational 4, Lutheran 1, Catholic 1. [SL20]

**v. 13 (who is the angel?):** The Geneva Study Bible (Reformed) names him Christ. [BH13] Calvin is more careful: either God the Father showing himself through his Word, or an angel speaking on his behalf. [SL13]

## 3. Other views

**Ancient translations and Augustine (v. 7):** The Septuagint reads "ten lambs." Augustine took this to mean five years of wages, as reported by Clarke. [SL7]

**Jewish tradition (v. 19):** Clarke reports a strange explanation in the Targum of Jonathan (an ancient Aramaic paraphrase): the teraphim were the embalmed head of a firstborn son that "conversed" with Laban. [SL19] Guzik and Coffman mention a Jewish midrash that Rachel wanted to cure her father of idolatry. [EW], [SL19]

**Archaeology (v. 19):** Coffman cites Henry Morris on the Nuzi tablets, which link teraphim to inheritance and property rights. On that reading, Rachel may have thought owning them would support Jacob's claim to the flocks. [SL19] The biblehub study page says the same about a possible inheritance claim. [BHS19]

**Source criticism (vv. 10–13, 18):** A note on the biblehub page credits a verse in this section to the "P" source (the "priestly" strand some scholars see in Genesis), citing its wording and repetition. [BH15] The Pulpit Commentary disagrees that the account of the dream points to different sources; it says the difference reflects what actually happened. [BH13]

**Dating the dream (vv. 10–13):** Coffman notes that the Samaritan version places the whole dream after Genesis 30:36, at the start of the six years. [SL13]

**Not found:** I found nothing on these verses from NET Bible notes, Bible Odyssey, Catholic or Orthodox sites, or prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching, so I've left those out.
